lead: Mains arrives as 230 V, 50 Hz AC. Almost every circuit inside a phone, TV or laptop needs steady DC. A rectifier bridges the two: it uses diodes, which conduct in one direction only, to convert AC into pulsating DC. A filter then flattens the pulses (chapter 1.2) and a regulator holds the level steady. Half-wave, centre-tapped full-wave and bridge are the three standard circuits. The bridge is the most common in real products because it needs no centre-tapped transformer. Some syllabi call the bridge the Graetz rectifier.
prereq: You need: the PN junction diode's one-way conduction and its 0.7 V silicon drop, the ideal-diode model, and the link between rms and peak for a sine wave, Vm = √2 × Vrms.

sections.h3: The half-wave rectifier: one diode, one half cycle

blocks.text: Connect the transformer secondary, one diode and the load resistor R in series. In the positive half cycle the anode is positive, the diode conducts, and the secondary voltage appears across R minus the diode drop. In the negative half cycle the diode is reverse biased, no current flows, and the load voltage is zero. The output is a row of positive humps, not a steady DC.

Let Vm be the peak secondary voltage in volts, R the load in ohms, and Vd the diode forward drop: 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium. The transformer is rated in rms, so Vm = 1.414 × Vrms. The humps repeat once per supply cycle, so the ripple frequency equals the supply frequency.

blocks.where: Vdc is the average load voltage in volts; Vm is the peak secondary voltage in volts; π = 3.1416. With a real diode, replace Vm by (Vm − Vd).
Im is the peak load current in amperes; R is the load resistance in ohms; Irms is the rms current in the diode and load over one full cycle.

items: Peak inverse voltage: PIV = Vm. The reverse-biased diode must survive the whole secondary peak.
Ripple frequency = 50 Hz for a 50 Hz supply.
Maximum rectification efficiency η = Pdc/Pac = 40.6 %, the worst of the three circuits.
Transformer utilisation factor TUF = DC power delivered ÷ secondary VA rating = 0.287.

blocks.text: The centre-tap circuit uses a secondary with a middle connection, giving two equal halves of peak Vm each. D1 conducts on the positive half cycle and D2 on the negative, but both push current through R in the same direction. The load now sees one hump every half cycle, so the ripple frequency is 2f = 100 Hz and the DC output doubles.

blocks.where: Vm is the peak of one half of the secondary, measured from the centre tap to one end, not the whole secondary.

blocks.text: The PIV here is 2Vm, not Vm. When D1 conducts, the other end of the secondary swings to −Vm, so the non-conducting D2 faces Vm from its own half plus Vm from the conducting half.

The bridge rectifier removes the centre tap. Four diodes form a ring; opposite pairs conduct on alternate half cycles, so the load current keeps the same direction. The secondary is used fully in both halves, which is why its TUF (0.812) beats the centre tap (0.693). The price is two diode drops in the conducting path instead of one.

blocks.where: Vm is the peak of the full secondary; the 2Vd accounts for two forward-biased diodes in series with the load. Ideal full-wave efficiency is 81.2 %, but the bridge's is a little lower in practice because of that extra drop.

items: Find the secondary rms: primary rms ÷ turns ratio.
Convert to peak: Vm = 1.414 × secondary rms.
Subtract the diode drops that actually sit in the conducting path: one for half-wave and centre tap, two for a bridge.
Apply the Vdc formula for that circuit.
Set the ripple frequency to f or 2f.
Read PIV from the reverse-biased diode, remembering the centre-tap case doubles it.

figure.caption: The rectifier sits between the step-down transformer and the filter. Notice that the rectifier block is the only one that changes AC to one-way current; the filter only smooths it.

examples.question: A 230 V, 50 Hz mains supply is stepped down by a 10:1 transformer and fed to a half-wave rectifier with a 1 kΩ load and a silicon diode (Vd = 0.7 V). Find the peak load voltage, the DC load voltage, the ripple frequency and the PIV of the diode.
steps: Peak load voltage = Vm − Vd = 32.53 − 0.7 = 31.83 V.
Peak load current Im = 31.83 V / 1000 Ω = 31.83 mA.
DC load voltage Vdc = Vm(load) / π = 31.83 / 3.1416 = 10.13 V.
DC load current Idc = 10.13 V / 1000 Ω = 10.13 mA.
Ripple frequency = supply frequency = 50 Hz, because one hump appears per cycle.
PIV = reverse peak across the diode = full secondary peak = 32.53 V (the load drop does not appear across it).
examples.answer: Peak load voltage 31.83 V, DC load voltage 10.13 V, ripple frequency 50 Hz, PIV 32.53 V.
examples.check:
import math
Vp = 230.0
n = 10.0
Vd = 0.7
R = 1000.0
Vm = math.sqrt(2) * Vp / n
VmL = Vm - Vd
Vdc = VmL / math.pi
Idc = Vdc / R
print(round(VmL, 2))
print(round(Vdc, 2))
print(50)
print(round(Vm, 2))

code.code:
import math
Vp=230.0; n=10.0; Vd=0.7; R=1000.0
Vm=math.sqrt(2)*Vp/n
VmL=Vm-Vd
Vdc=VmL/math.pi
print('peak load V =', round(VmL,2))
print('Vdc =', round(Vdc,2))
print('ripple Hz =', 50)
print('PIV =', round(Vm,2))

examples.output:
peak load V = 31.83
Vdc = 10.13
ripple Hz = 50
PIV = 32.53

traps: Putting the rms value into Vdc = Vm/π. The formula wants the peak; 23 V rms gives 32.53 V peak, and the DC is 10.13 V, not 7.32 V.
Forgetting the diode drop. Subtract 0.7 V from the peak before dividing by π; subtracting it after division gives the wrong answer.
Saying the bridge PIV is 2Vm. In a bridge, each reverse diode sees only Vm. The 2Vm figure belongs to the centre-tap circuit.
Using 0.636 Vm for a half-wave rectifier. That constant is for full-wave; half-wave is 0.318 Vm.
Reporting 50 Hz ripple for a full-wave circuit. Both full-wave types double the ripple frequency to 100 Hz.

quiz.q: State the ripple frequency of a half-wave and of a full-wave rectifier fed from a 50 Hz supply.
quiz.a: Half-wave: 50 Hz, one hump per cycle. Full-wave (centre-tap or bridge): 100 Hz, one hump per half cycle.

quiz.q: Give the maximum rectification efficiency of the half-wave and the full-wave rectifier.
Why is the PIV of a centre-tap rectifier 2Vm while that of a bridge is only Vm?
quiz.a: In the centre-tap circuit the non-conducting diode is connected to one end of the secondary while the other end is pulled to −Vm by the conducting diode, so it sees Vm + Vm = 2Vm. In a bridge each reverse diode is across the secondary through a conducting diode, so it sees only Vm.

quiz.q: Why is the rectifier output called pulsating DC and not AC?
quiz.a: The current never reverses, so the waveform has a non-zero average, which is DC. Its magnitude still varies between zero and Vm, so it is pulsating rather than steady.

quiz.q: A 12-0-12 V centre-tapped secondary (12 V rms from centre to each end) feeds a full-wave rectifier with a 1 kΩ load and silicon diodes of Vd = 0.7 V. Find Vdc and the ripple frequency.
A bridge rectifier runs from a 20 V rms secondary with Vd = 0.7 V per diode and a 1 kΩ load. Find Vdc, PIV and Idc.
quiz.a: Vm = 1.414 × 20 = 28.28 V. Two diodes conduct, so peak load = 28.28 − 1.4 = 26.88 V. Vdc = 2 × 26.88/π = 17.12 V. Idc = 17.12 mA. PIV = Vm = 28.28 V.

quiz.q: The transformer utilisation factor of a bridge is 0.812 against 0.693 for a centre tap. Explain why.
quiz.a: In a centre-tap circuit each half winding carries current for only half of every cycle, so the secondary VA rating must be larger for the same DC power. In a bridge the whole secondary conducts in both halves, so the same winding delivers more DC power per volt-ampere. The bridge also avoids the extra copper of a centre tap.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real chargers put a bridge straight after the mains filter, and above roughly 100 W the diodes are Schottky types to cut the forward drop and the loss. In high-voltage chargers and inverters, silicon-carbide diodes are chosen because they recover faster. Designers also work on bridgeless power-factor-correction front ends that remove the bridge loss entirely. Search next: bridge rectifier heat sinking, diode reverse recovery, bridgeless PFC.
